full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs-respondent No.1 Mrs. Arzuda Khatun instituted the above title suit against the defendant-petitioner Mrs. Nazma Begum and others for a declaration of her title and recovery of khas possession of the suit property. The plaintiffs case was that she took lease from of the property from erstwhile Government of East Pakistan by a lease deed no. 6327 dated 05.10.1968 and since then she was possessing the same. During the war of liberation she had to leave her house on the suit land leaving her deeds etc. there in order to save her life and on return after liberation found that the defendant-petitioner had illegally entered into the possession of the same. She failed in her attempts to get back the possession of the said property and therefore constrained to bring the above suit for declaration of her title and recovery of khas possession. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge passed the judgment on 27.09.1998 where after the decree .was prepared and signed on 06.10.1998. The decree was drawn in accordance with the ordering portion of the judgment i.e. in the decree plaintiff's title was declared and nothing was said about the prayer for recovery of khas possession. The plaintiff-respondent No.1 Arzuda Khatun on 08.11.1998 filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge praying for amendment of the judgment and decree incorporating the relief of khas possession in her favour and the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 12.11.1998 allowed the prayer for amendment of the judgment and decree and accordingly the judgment and the decree were amended. 

 9. The High Court Division also correctly took into the submission made by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent that the Court can correct any error or omission covered by section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure even suo-motu and as such it was not obligatory upon the court to give notice upon the defendant petitioner before amendment of mistake or omission. These views find support in the decision reported in 22 DLR 130. A decree should be consistent with the plaint in the absence of an indication that particular relief has been refused. A matter in issue decided by the court must be included in the decree and if not included it may be corrected on an application of amendment of the decree. Every Court has an inherent power to very or amend its own decree or order so as to carry out its own meaning. In the instant case, the court having found in favour of the plaintiff-respondent as to the title in the suit land and the plaintiff was out of possession the decree would be of no use to the plaintiff unless the ordering portion of the judgment included an order for recovery of khas possession by the plaintiff. The High Court Division therefore discharged the Rule.
